content.thinking:
I need to frame this as a monitoring blind spot with no clear customer impact, and I should avoid restating any specific figures like duration or error rate as if I'd calculated them myself—those numbers were given, not derived.

For root cause, my leading hypothesis is that a deploy renamed the metrics port but the scrape config still referenced the old name, causing the scraper to lose its target—though this is unverified at roughly 0.88 confidence and I need to flag it as an assumption. I should also note other open assumptions: the error rate is unknown, the fix exists only as an unmerged draft PR, and the log evidence for benign client disconnects is inferred rather than confirmed.

Application logs actually continue past 10:15 through 10:20, showing normal rendering and routine client disconnects, which weakly supports the service being healthy even though it's less reliable than metrics-based evidence.

assumptions: The root cause is the investigator's leading hypothesis (port rename breaking the scrape target) at 0.88 confidence. It was never tested: no mitigation was attempted and the proposed fix is still a draft pull request, so metrics were not observed to return.

The alternative reading — that the port rename was accidental rather than an intentional estate-wide convention — fits the same evidence and was not ruled out. It changes the remediation and process follow-up, not the technical failure mode.

The service is assumed to have been healthy during the unobserved window on the strength of its log lines alone (normal rendering and client-initiated disconnects). No metrics exist for that window, so the error rate during the incident is unknown and the usual error-rate evidence cannot confirm or contradict this.
The client-side disconnect errors in the logs are assumed to be background noise unrelated to the incident; they appear both before and after the onset minute at similar frequency.
Only two production changes in the preceding day were reviewed, and the feature-flag provider reported no recent flag changes, so the 10:15 deploy is assumed to be the only plausible trigger.
Scope is assumed to be io-shop only; no check was made for other services affected by the same naming convention change.
input.executive_summary:
Starting at the moment of a routine software update on the morning of 5 October, the shop's account pages stopped reporting their health to our monitoring systems. The pages themselves appear to have kept working normally throughout — the service's own activity records continue uninterrupted and show nothing worse than the usual pattern of shoppers closing their browsers mid-request — so there is no indication that any customer was affected. The gap was in what we could see, not in what customers got.

Monitoring remained blind from the update onwards and was still blind when the incident was closed out; the outage of visibility was short, but it was not restored during the incident itself. An automated responder picked the alert up within minutes, read the service's recent activity records and recent production changes, and determined that the update had changed an internal label that the monitoring system relies on to find the service. No automated mitigation was applicable, so the responder opened a draft code change for a human to review and merge, and escalated to the on-call team.

Outstanding work: review and merge the proposed change so metrics collection resumes, confirm metrics actually return, and check whether other services touched by the same naming change are silently unmonitored. The automated responder's own handling time is a measure of the response, not of how long the service was unobserved, and should not be read as the latter.
input.root_cause: The 10:15:00Z deploy to io-shop renamed the container's metrics port from `metrics` to `http-metrics` (apparently as part of an estate-wide naming convention), but the scrape configuration still selects the target by the old port name, so the Prometheus-style scraper dropped io-shop as a target at the onset minute. The application itself appears to have kept serving — its logs continue through and after the deploy with only routine client-side disconnects and normal rendering — so this was a loss of observability rather than a loss of service.
